items.title: LM Studio Bionic: Local Agentic AI Experiments
items.description: LM Studio Bionic installed and tested on modest PC hardware, and then used to run local AI models for agentic web access and document manipulation. items.title: AI & the Future of the Web
items.description: Will AI destroy the web? In this video I discuss how this may slowly occur as AI disrupts the web’s search-and-visit business model, we transition from GUIs to agentic computing interfaces, and generative AI really takes hold . . . My related video on "AI & the Future of Film Making" on the @christopherbarnatt channel is here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=mjtASnfuMTg My recent video on “The Future of Home Computing is also here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=oJe2IOO1224 And the first ever @ExplainingComputers video -- “Explaining Web 2.0” -- is here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=7BAXvFdMBWw All of my videos on the future of computing can also be found on this page: https://explainingcomputers.com/future_computing.html More videos on film and other making, plus retro tech, can be found on my Christopher Barnatt channel: http://www.youtube.com/@ChristopherBarnatt Chapters: 00:00 Titles & Intro 00:39 Disrupting Search & Visit 03:20 Agentic Interfaces 06:11 AI Content 08:56 The Demise of Social Media 10:42 Decreasing Text Centricity 13:00 Beyond Web 2.0 #AI #web #www #agents #agenticAI

items.title: Running Gemma 4 Local AI
items.description: How to run Gemma 4 open local AI models in LM Studio on a computer with integrated graphics (like most laptops and mini PCs). Although everything here will also work just fine on a system with a dedicated graphics card. You can download the version of LM Studio shown in the video here: https://lmstudio.ai/download -- where is the SECOND download on offer. I note this because, in the days since the video was made, a new agentic application called "LM Studio Bionic" was released, and it is this program that is now linked on the LM Studio homepage and is now listed first on the download page. If you enjoy this video, you may also like my episode on Agentic AI: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Gvt4TwGpqOs CONFIGURATION NOTES There are lots of settings that you can experiment with when running LLMs like Gemma 4 locally, especially if you have a powerful dedicated GPU with a lot of VRAM. But on my system with integrated graphics, I experimented with the following changes: CONTEXT LENGTH: Go to “My Models”, click on the gear icon to access the settings for a particular model, and then click on the “Load” tab. Here you can set the “Context Length” for a model, which on my system for Gemma 4 12B defaulted to 8192 tokens. However, I tried reducing this to 4096 to save resources and increase speed. But I put this back to 8196 for the test summarizing the 3900 word book chapter. CPU THREAD POOL SIZE: in the settings for a model, under the “Inference” tab you will find a control for the “CPU Thread Pool Size”, which by default on my system was set to 4. I increased this to 6, which is the number of physical CPU cores in my Ryzen 5600G processor, and setting the CPU Thread Pool Size to your number of physical CPU cores is often advised. Having made these two changes, I obtained a slight increase in tokens a second. But it was very slight, and less than the variance when running different tasks. So because of this I chose not to include a section in the video explaining this. The video was already long, and I thought it better to get to the practical use of Gemma 4 five minutes earlier! :) I also conducted many experiments with my BIOS settings in attempt to run all or part of a Gemma 4 model on the 5600G’s integrated GPU (iGPU). But Gemma 4 12B QAT cannot be partially “offloaded”, and there are limits on the amount of RAM that an iGPU can access (well, at least on older/traditional hardware ike a 5600G APU). Using the GPU Offload setting, I did manage to offload part of the Gemma 4 E4B Q_K_M model to the iGPU, but with no practical advantage (due I imagine to the model remaining in the same RAM, and bottle necks being created with the model split between the CPU and GPU). I did find it beneficial to off-load the model’s Key-Value (KV) cache to the GPU, and did this with a fixed 2GB RAM allocated to the iGPU. My conclusion this far is to trust LM Studio to get the settings right, and only to adjust the Context Length when required to process large text files. --- You can access most ExplainingComputers videos by category from this page: https://explainingcomputers.com/videos.html More videos on film and other making, plus retro tech, can be found on my Christopher Barnatt channel: http://www.youtube.com/@ChristopherBarnatt Chapters: 00:00 Titles & Intro 00:56 Choosing Your Model 04:25 LM Studio 08:51 Speed & Application 13:55 Images & Text Files 17:20 Coding 18:57 Gemma 4 E4B 21:31 Wrap #Gemma4 #12B #E4B #LMStudio #LocalAI

items.title: Milk-V Jupiter 2: RISC-V RVA23 SBC
items.description: Milk-V Jupiter 2 review -- including specifications, demos and benchmarks of this Spacemit K3 Pico-ITX, RVA23-compliant RISC-V computer. You can learn more about the Milk-V Jupiter 2 on its web page here: https://milkv.io/jupiter2 My 2023 video in which I only used RISC-V hardware for a week is here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=Na6PT4npsMg I look forward to repeating this test with the Milk-V Jupiter 2! items.title: Top 10 Extinct Storage Media: How many do you know?
items.description: Ten removable storage media -- including floppy disks, hard drive cartridges, and magneto-optical disks -- that were released between 1971 and 1998. But how many do you know? Or even remember using?! My video on making animation at the BBC in the 1980s and 1990s, where I first encountered 8 inch floppy disks, is here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=TkOOMYWgn14 My previous video on the Atari Portfolio is also here: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-B_GaZDkhU0 And all of my retro computing videos are linked on this page: https://explainingcomputers.com/classic_computers.html SELECTED REFERENCES: For the interested, further information on some of the media featured in this video can be found as follows: IBM page on the invention of floppy disks: https://www.ibm.com/history/floppy-disk IBM System 3740 brochure: http://bitsavers.informatik.uni-stuttgart.de/pdf/ibm/brochures/IBM3740DataEntrySystem.pdf Excellent RetroCMP page on floppy disks: https://retrocmp.de/fdd/diskette/diskette.htm 8 inch floppy disks retired by US military in 2019: https://www.popularmechanics.com/military/a29539578/air-force-floppy-disks/ Fuji 2 inch floppy disks: https://www.storagenewsletter.com/2018/11/06/history-1989-2-inch-floppy-disk-lt-1-made-by-fujifilm/ Excellent Maxoptix page on the state-of-play of magneto-optical discs: https://maxoptix.com/the-state-of-magneto-optical-discs/ Sony 3.5 inch MO Discs brochure: https://pro.sony/s3/cms-static-content/file/58/1237486481358.pdf Sony 5.25 inch MO Discs brochure: https://pro.sony/s3/cms-static-content/file/72/1237486492172.pdf Sony MDH-10 MD-Data data drive: https://www.minidisc.org/part_Sony_MDH-10.html More videos on computing and related topics can be found at: http://www.youtube.com/@ExplainingComputers And more videos on film and other making, plus retro tech, can be found on my Christopher Barnatt channel: http://www.youtube.com/@ChristopherBarnatt Chapters: 00:00 Titles & Intro 00:36 Floppy Days 06:24 SyQuest vs Iomega 12:39 Solid State 14:35 Magneto-Optical 10:45 Our Binary Containers 18:13 End of an Era #floppydisk #SyQuest #Iomega #Zipdisk #Jazdisk #DVD-RAM #MDData #AtartPorfolio #retrostorage #retrocomputing
